newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dikes in flood-hit east Germany still at risk.
newsitem.headline: Dikes in flood-hit east Germany still at risk.

text.p: The situation along the flood-hit River Oder on the German-Polish border remained critical on Wednesday, officials in east Germany said, warning residents not to be complacent.

Earlier, floods showed signs of receding after a fresh high-water surge expected overnight did not materialise. They said many flood-barriers reinforcing the river were extremely porous, riddled with weak spots that could give way any time.
"We are still far from winning the game," said Manfred Stolpe, the premier of the state of Brandenburg -- part of which has been devastated by the worst floods for centuries.
The floods have hit Poland and the Czech republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

Stolpe thanked the thousands of soldiers, aid workers and volunteers for their efforts sandbagging around the clock during the last week. "Without their help the dikes would have collapsed long ago," he said.

He said Brandenburg was grateful for some two million marks collected across Germany and said his regional government and the federal authorities in Bonn had pooled together an extra 40 million marks in flood relief.
The European Union (EU) announced it would set aside 1.5 million Ecu in relief aid to help the devastated region.
Stolpe said this could contribute toward a possible joint project with Poland to rebuild the flood barriers along both sides of the River Oder to avert any future disasters.
Bonn has already set aside a fund of 200 million in aid for reconstruction of the beleaguered region on the floods subside.

Local officials said the situation was tense near the village of Neuruednitz where soldiers were sandbagging to prevent flooding in the low-lying Oderbruch area, where some 5,000 of the 19,000 inhabitants were evacuated last week.

Oderbruch, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago to create fertile farmland and is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
The Oder dikes have not failed since 1947, when floods wrought havoc around the town of Reitwein, north of Frankfurt an der Oder.
German Army First lieutenant Mike Burmester, in charge of three groups of soldiers repairing the dikes, said: "The dike would have burst many times by now".

Local resident Martin Nabaum, 58, who had been monitoring water levels for the last 40 hours, said: "The water has risen two cm since 6 a.m. If the flood barrier breaks I'll lose all of my possessions. Why should I stay home."
Udo Eckner, 33, said the worst thing was that people were getting complacent: "You get used to a catastrophe after a while. The first few days were really bad, but man is a creature of habit".
Ecker said there were dozens of places along the dike, drenched and weakened by nearly two weeks of flooding, where water was seeping through its foundations.

"It's as if you were to wring out a washcloth. When the water comes through brownish carrying bits and pieces of earth then we know it's serious and we have to fill the spot immediately with sandbags."
